language_convention_note: 'Person who stutters' is preferred by most stuttering organizations; many adults also say 'I'm a stutterer'. Both appear here.
one_liner: Repeating, prolonging, or getting stuck on sounds and words, starting in childhood, beyond ordinary hesitation.
in_simple_words: Stuttering is a difference in the flow of speech: sounds or syllables repeat, stretch out, or get stuck so no sound comes out. It usually starts between ages two and five and has nothing to do with intelligence, nerves, or parenting. Most young children who stutter stop within a few years; for about one in a hundred people it continues into adulthood. Therapy helps at every age, and many people who stutter decide the goal is speaking freely, stutter and all.
what_it_can_feel_like: It's not that I don't know the word. The word knows it's coming and the door slams.
I spent twenty years swapping words to avoid the hard ones. Therapy let me say my own name.
My son's stutter got worse when we told him to slow down. Then we learned to just listen.
common_signs: Stretching sounds out, or silent blocks where no sound comes
Visible tension, blinking, or movements while trying to speak
Avoiding certain words, situations, or speaking at all
Starting in early childhood and continuing beyond six months

myths_vs_facts.myth: Stuttering is caused by anxiety or shyness.
myths_vs_facts.fact: Stuttering is neurological and often runs in families. Anxiety can make it worse, but it doesn't cause it.

myths_vs_facts.myth: Telling someone to slow down or take a breath helps.
myths_vs_facts.fact: It usually adds pressure. Giving time, keeping eye contact, and not finishing sentences is what helps.

myths_vs_facts.myth: People who stutter are less intelligent or confident.
myths_vs_facts.fact: Stuttering has no link to intelligence. Many people who stutter are confident public speakers, actors, and leaders.

how_common.plain: About 5 to 8 in every 100 children stutter at some point, usually starting between two and five. Around 1 in 100 adults stutters, with men affected about four times as often as women.
how_common.figure: Onset in at least 5% of children; persists in about 1% of the general population after puberty; male-to-female ratio about 4:1

what_helps.plain_summary: For young children, therapy that coaches parents in responding to stuttering (for example the Lidcombe or Palin approaches) has good evidence and often leads to recovery. For older children and adults, speech therapy teaches techniques for easier speech and, just as important, reduces fear and avoidance so the person can say what they want to say. Peer support from other people who stutter is powerful. There is no medication for stuttering.
evidence_based_options: Parent-led early intervention programmes for preschool children
Speech and language therapy for older children and adults, combining fluency techniques with confidence and acceptance work
CBT for the anxiety and avoidance that can build up around stuttering
Self-help and peer support groups run by stuttering organizations
self_help_that_supports_care: Saying what you want to say, not swapping words
Telling people you stutter, which takes the pressure off
Connecting with other people who stutter
For listeners: wait, keep natural eye contact, don't finish sentences

when_to_reach_out: If a child's stuttering has lasted more than six months, started after age three and a half, runs in the family, or is causing distress or avoidance, ask for a speech and language therapy assessment; don't wait and see for too long. Adults can seek therapy at any age.
is_not: Everyone hesitates, repeats whole words, or says 'um' sometimes, especially when tired or excited; that's normal non-fluency. Stuttering that begins in adulthood after a brain injury, stroke, or severe stress is a different condition and needs medical assessment.
hope_note: Whether speech becomes smoother or not, people who stutter learn to say everything they want to say, and the world is slowly learning to listen.
strengths_and_differences: Many people who stutter describe becoming careful listeners, thoughtful speakers, and resilient advocates. The stuttering community has a strong, proud culture of its own.
in_young_people: Stuttering usually begins between two and five, often when language is developing fast. Early therapy works best, and it's gentle and play-based. Schools should know, so the child isn't marked down for not reading aloud.

sub_sections.title: Adult-onset fluency disorder
sub_sections.text: Stuttering that starts in adulthood, usually after a neurological event or severe psychological stress. Needs medical assessment to find the cause.
